title: Discriminated Unions
summary: A **discriminated (tagged) union** is a union of object types that all share a common *literal* field — the *discriminant* (e.g. `kind` or `status`). Switching on that tag lets TypeScript narrow to exactly one variant, and a `never` check makes the `switch` exhaustive. It's the type-safe way to model state and replace fragile optional-field 'soup'.

subtopics.title: The discriminant tag
subtopics.explanation: Each member of the union has a shared property whose type is a unique string (or numeric) literal — the discriminant. Because the tags are distinct literals, TypeScript can tell members apart just by reading that one field, no other check needed.
subtopics.example:
type A = { kind: 'a'; x: number };
type B = { kind: 'b'; y: string };

subtopics.title: Narrowing by the discriminant
subtopics.explanation: Checking the tag (if (s.kind === 'a') or a switch case) narrows the value to the single matching variant. Inside that branch you can access that variant's unique fields safely — the others are eliminated from the type.
subtopics.example: if (s.kind === 'a') s.x; // only A's fields available

subtopics.title: Exhaustive switch
subtopics.explanation: A switch over the discriminant with one case per variant handles every possibility. Adding a default that asserts never turns 'I forgot a case' into a compile error, so the switch is provably exhaustive.

subtopics.title: never & assertNever
subtopics.explanation: When all variants are handled, the value's type in the default branch is never. Passing it to assertNever(x: never) compiles only while exhaustive; introduce a new variant and the call errors, pointing at the missing case.
subtopics.example: function assertNever(x: never): never { throw new Error(String(x)); }

subtopics.title: Modeling state (loading/success/error)
subtopics.explanation: Async state is the textbook use: a union of { status: 'loading' } | { status: 'success'; data: T } | { status: 'error'; error: string }. Each state carries exactly the data that's valid for it — data exists only on success, error only on error.
subtopics.example: type State<T> = { status: 'loading' } | { status: 'success'; data: T } | { status: 'error'; error: string };

subtopics.title: Why they beat optional-field soup
subtopics.explanation: A single type with isLoading?, data?, error? all optional allows impossible states (loading and error at once; success with no data). A discriminated union makes only valid combinations representable, so 'make impossible states unrepresentable' is enforced by the compiler.
subtopics.example: // bad: { isLoading?: boolean; data?: T; error?: string }

subtopics.title: Reducers & events
subtopics.explanation: Discriminated unions model reducer actions and event payloads: each action has a unique type tag plus its own payload shape. The reducer's switch narrows per action and the never default guarantees every action is handled.
subtopics.example: type Action = { type: 'inc'; by: number } | { type: 'reset' };

foundations.overview: A discriminated union (also called a tagged union or algebraic data type) is a union of object types that all share a common property — the discriminant — typed as a unique literal in each member. Because the discriminant values are disjoint literals, TypeScript can narrow the union to one exact member just by checking that field. This makes switches over the tag both ergonomic and, with a never check, exhaustive. Discriminated unions are the idiomatic way to model anything that has distinct, mutually-exclusive states with state-specific data.
foundations.formalDefinition: A discriminated union is a union type U = M1 | M2 | ... | Mn where every Mi is an object type containing a common property d whose type in Mi is a singleton literal Li, and the Li are pairwise distinct. Narrowing on d refines U to the unique Mi with d === Li.
foundations.whyItMatters: They are the canonical tool for 'make impossible states unrepresentable' — eliminating bugs where contradictory flags coexist. They power Redux actions, async state, parser results, and Result/Either types, and are a staple advanced interview topic because they tie together unions, literals, narrowing, and never.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the discriminant as a label on a sealed box. You read only the label (the tag) to know exactly which box you have and therefore exactly what's inside — no peeking at the other fields, no guessing.
foundations.browserPerspective: Purely compile-time. The discriminant field is a real runtime property (a string/number you can read in the browser), but the narrowing and exhaustiveness checks are erased — the emitted JS is just a normal switch on a property.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Async fetch state (loading/success/error), Redux/useReducer actions, WebSocket/message protocols, parser or validation results (ok/err), shape hierarchies (circle/square), and any finite-state model.
foundations.businessImpact: By making contradictory states impossible at the type level, discriminated unions prevent a class of UI bugs (e.g. showing a spinner and an error simultaneously) that directly affect user trust and support volume.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Adding a new variant is a guided refactor: the never exhaustiveness check flags every switch that must handle it, so the compiler drives correctness instead of relying on memory and review.
foundations.performanceImpact: Zero runtime cost beyond a cheap property read in a switch. The win is fewer defensive runtime checks because invalid combinations can't exist.
commonUseCases: Async data state: loading | success | error
Result/Either types: { ok: true; value } | { ok: false; error }
Shape or message hierarchies narrowed by a kind/type tag

commonMisconceptions.myth: Any union of objects is a discriminated union.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only unions whose members share a common property typed as distinct literals are discriminated; without that shared literal tag, TypeScript can't narrow by a single field check.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should use optional fields with flags instead.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Optional-field 'soup' allows impossible combinations (loading + error, success with no data). A discriminated union makes only valid states representable.
TypeScript only enforces exhaustiveness if you add a never check (e.g. assertNever in the default); otherwise a missing case can silently fall through.

debuggingLab.title: Optional-field soup allows impossible states
debuggingLab.symptom: A state object with all-optional flags lets contradictory combinations exist, so the UI can show data and an error at once, and TypeScript can't help.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: With all fields optional and independent, the type permits contradictory states: data and error set together, or loading while data exists. TypeScript can't enforce mutual exclusivity, so rendering logic relies on brittle if-ordering and impossible states slip through.
commonMistakes: Using one interface with optional flags instead of distinct variants.
Relying on if-ordering to fake mutual exclusivity between states.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Replace the soup with a discriminated union on status so only valid state combinations are representable, and handle them with an exhaustive switch.

theory.question: What is a discriminated union and what makes it 'discriminated'?
theory.directAnswer: It's a union of object types that all share a common property — the discriminant — typed as a unique literal in each member (e.g. kind: 'circle' | kind: 'square'). It's 'discriminated' because TypeScript can tell the members apart by reading that single field: checking the tag narrows the union to exactly one variant, exposing only that variant's fields.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A union whose members carry a shared, distinct literal tag that the compiler narrows on.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To model mutually-exclusive states/variants where each carries its own data, while letting the compiler narrow and check exhaustively.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Because the discriminant values are disjoint literals, a check on that property (if/switch) refines the union to the single matching member; the analysis is erased at runtime.

theory.whyImportant: It ties together unions, literal types, narrowing, and never, and is the idiomatic pattern for state, actions, and results — a frequent advanced interview topic.
theory.realWorldExample: An async State union loading | success | error switched on status.

followUps.question: What requirement must the shared field meet?
followUps.answer: Its type in each member must be a unique singleton literal (string or number); shared non-literal types can't discriminate because the compiler can't distinguish members by value.

followUps.question: Can the discriminant be a boolean?
followUps.answer: Yes — a Result type often uses ok: true | ok: false, which are distinct boolean literals the compiler can narrow on.

theory.question: How do discriminated unions enable exhaustiveness checking, and why prefer them over optional fields?
theory.directAnswer: Switch on the discriminant with one case per variant; in the default, the value's type is never once all cases are handled. Passing it to assertNever(x: never) compiles only while exhaustive, so adding a variant forces you to handle it everywhere. They beat optional-field soup because they make impossible states (e.g. loading and error together, success with no data) unrepresentable, instead of merely discouraged.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A pattern combining a tagged union, a switch, and a never assertion to guarantee complete, valid handling.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Optional-flag types permit contradictory combinations and silent missing cases; tagged unions and never close both gaps.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Narrowing removes handled variants until the leftover is never; never is assignable only to never, so an unhandled variant fails assertNever and flags the gap.

theory.whyImportant: It turns 'forgot a case' and 'invalid state' from runtime bugs into compile errors, which is the core value proposition of typing state.
theory.realWorldExample: A useReducer where every Action variant must be handled; adding a new action breaks the build until the reducer covers it.

nestedTopics.title: assertNever
nestedTopics.explanation: Centralizes the exhaustiveness assertion in the default branch.

nestedTopics.title: Make impossible states unrepresentable
nestedTopics.explanation: Each variant carries only its valid fields, so contradictions can't be constructed.

followUps.question: What if you don't add the never default?
followUps.answer: TypeScript won't force exhaustiveness; a missing case can silently fall through (returning undefined), so the never check is what makes completeness compiler-enforced.

scenario.question: A component models fetch state with isLoading, data, and error all optional, and occasionally renders a spinner over an error. How do you redesign it?
scenario.directAnswer: Replace the three optional fields with a discriminated union on status: { status: 'loading' } | { status: 'success'; data: T } | { status: 'error'; error: string }. Render via a switch on status with an assertNever default. Now data exists only on success and error only on error, so the spinner-over-error state is literally unconstructable and the compiler enforces handling every state.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Refactoring optional-field state into mutually-exclusive tagged variants.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: All-optional fields allow contradictory combinations the UI must defend against manually.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each status variant carries exactly its valid payload; switching on status narrows to one variant and the never default guarantees completeness.

scenario.whyImportant: Async UI state is one of the most common sources of inconsistent-UI bugs; a discriminated union eliminates them structurally rather than via careful coding.

nestedTopics.title: State machine framing
nestedTopics.explanation: The union is effectively a finite-state model of the request lifecycle.

nestedTopics.title: Exhaustive rendering
nestedTopics.explanation: A switch + assertNever ensures every state has a defined UI.

followUps.question: How would you add a 'refreshing' state without regressions?
followUps.answer: Add a new variant to the union; every switch with an assertNever default will fail to compile until it handles 'refreshing', so the compiler guides the rollout.

coding.question: Write a useReducer-style reducer over a discriminated Action union with an exhaustive switch.
coding.thoughtProcess: I'll define Action as a union tagged by type, each variant carrying its own payload. The reducer switches on action.type; each case narrows to that action so its payload fields are available and correctly typed. A default branch calls assertNever(action) so adding an action type without a case is a compile error.
coding.lineByLine: Action is a union tagged by type; increment/decrement carry a by payload, reset carries none. In the switch, each case narrows action to that variant, so action.by is available only where it exists. The default calls assertNever(action): since all types are handled, action is never there and it compiles. Add a 'set' action without a case and assertNever errors.

alternativeApproaches.title: Map of handlers
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A Record<Action['type'], handler> can replace the switch but loses the simple per-case narrowing and the straightforward never exhaustiveness check.

followUps.question: Why include the assertNever default?
followUps.answer: It forces exhaustiveness: if a new action variant is added and not handled, action won't be never in the default and assertNever fails to compile, flagging the missing case.

systemDesign.question: Design a type-safe client/server message protocol over WebSocket using discriminated unions, ensuring every message is handled and impossible payloads are unrepresentable.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Model the protocol as two discriminated unions — ClientMessage and ServerMessage — each tagged by a unique type literal with a per-message payload. The handler switches on type, narrowing to one message so only that payload is accessible, and a default assertNever guarantees every message type is handled. Adding a message variant breaks the build until handlers cover it, and contradictory payloads can't be constructed because each variant carries only its own fields.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A protocol layer where each message kind is a tagged variant in a union, narrowed in the dispatch handler.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Untyped or optional-field message bags allow malformed/contradictory payloads and let new message types go silently unhandled across many handlers.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Distinct type literals let the handler narrow per message; the never exhaustiveness check enforces full coverage; pairing with a runtime validator (e.g. checking type then validating the payload) bridges the untrusted wire boundary to the typed union.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Message protocols fan out across many handlers and evolve over time; discriminated unions plus exhaustiveness make protocol evolution a guided, compile-checked refactor and prevent invalid payloads — a real architectural safeguard at scale.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A collaborative editor sending { type: 'edit'; ops: Op[] } | { type: 'cursor'; pos: number } | { type: 'ping' }; the server dispatch switches on type with assertNever.

nestedTopics.title: Runtime validation boundary
nestedTopics.explanation: Wire data is untrusted; validate it (e.g. with a guard/Zod) into the typed union before narrowing.

nestedTopics.title: Versioning / evolution
nestedTopics.explanation: New message types trigger exhaustiveness errors, guiding handler updates across the codebase.

nestedTopics.title: Bidirectional protocols
nestedTopics.explanation: Separate ClientMessage and ServerMessage unions keep each direction's variants and payloads distinct.

followUps.question: How do you handle messages from untrusted clients safely?
followUps.answer: Don't trust the wire type alone: validate the raw message at the boundary (check the type tag, then validate its payload shape with a runtime validator) to produce a value that actually conforms to the union before narrowing on it.

followUps.question: How does this scale as the protocol grows to dozens of message types?
followUps.answer: The assertNever exhaustiveness check makes every new message type a compile error in any handler that doesn't cover it, so the compiler — not code review — ensures all handlers stay complete.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Discriminated unions are the backbone of state modeling: Redux/useReducer actions, async request state, Result/Either error handling, and message protocols. Each domain concept becomes a union of tagged variants narrowed in a switch, giving a finite-state-machine-like structure the compiler can check.
productionDeepDive.performance: Negligible runtime cost — a switch on a property. The real gain is fewer defensive runtime checks because invalid states can't be constructed, reducing both code and branches.
productionDeepDive.security: At trust boundaries (network, storage, user input), validate raw data into the union with a runtime check before narrowing; the type system trusts the discriminant, so an unvalidated forged tag could misroute logic.
productionDeepDive.scaling: The never exhaustiveness check makes adding a variant a compiler-guided refactor across every handler, so large protocols and reducer sets stay complete as the system grows.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Centralize assertNever and use consistent discriminant names (kind/status/type). Prefer distinct variants over optional flags so impossible states are unrepresentable and intent is explicit.
productionDeepDive.observability: tsc --noEmit in CI catches missing cases via assertNever before runtime. Logging the discriminant tag of unexpected messages aids debugging at the validation boundary.

caseStudies.problem: Async state with isLoading/data/error flags produced contradictory UI states and missed action handling.
caseStudies.solution: Model state and actions as discriminated unions with exhaustive switches and assertNever.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more type boilerplate per variant vs. compiler-enforced valid states and complete handling.
caseStudies.lessons: Tagged unions plus never turn whole classes of state bugs into compile errors.

keyTakeaways: A discriminated union is a union of object types sharing a common literal tag (the discriminant).
Checking the tag (if/switch) narrows the union to exactly one variant, exposing only its fields.
An assertNever default makes a switch provably exhaustive — adding a variant becomes a compile error until handled.
They make impossible states unrepresentable, beating optional-field 'soup' where contradictory flags can coexist.
They are the idiomatic model for async state, Redux/useReducer actions, Result types, and message protocols.
